headline: Encrypt to a post-quantum and a classical key at once, so one broken primitive does not open the message.
summary: HPKE gains the three PQ/T hybrid KEMs: MLKEM768-P256, MLKEM1024-P384 and MLKEM768-X25519, which is X-Wing under the name the CFRG concrete-hybrid-KEMs draft gave it. Each pairs an ML-KEM with a nominal group and mixes both shared secrets into one, so the message stays closed unless both components are broken. `pki.hpke.seal` and `open` take them like any other suite, and `deriveKeyPair`, `generateKeyPair`, `encap` and `decap` reach a KEM on its own.

Added: The HPKE PQ/T hybrid KEMs MLKEM768-P256 (0x0050), MLKEM1024-P384 (0x0051) and MLKEM768-X25519 (0x647a), in the base and psk modes with every KDF and AEAD the module already offers. A hybrid decapsulation key is a 32-byte seed that both component keys expand from; its encapsulated key and ciphertext are the ML-KEM component followed by the group component. The shared secret is the CFRG C2PRI combiner, SHA3-256 over the ML-KEM secret, the group secret, the group ciphertext, the group public key and the suite label. All three are verified against the draft-irtf-cfrg-concrete-hybrid-kems Appendix B known-answer vectors, which pin the combiner's exact preimage: the ML-KEM ciphertext and public key are not bound, ML-KEM being ciphertext-collision-resistant already, and binding them would derive a different secret from the same exchange.

`pki.hpke.deriveKeyPair(kemId, ikm)`, `generateKeyPair(kemId)`, `encap(kemId, publicKey)` and `decap(kemId, enc, privateKey)` expose the KEM without a key schedule over it, for a caller building its own. They work for every KEM the module registers, not only the hybrids. `deriveKeyPair` is the KEM's own `DeriveKeyPair`: input keying material, run through the derivation its specification defines, so the pair matches what any other conforming implementation derives from the same input. It is checked against the published ikm-to-key vectors of RFC 9180 and draft-ietf-hpke-pq for every suite. To use a private key you already hold, pass it as `{ skm }` to `decap`, `setupR` or `open`.

MLKEM768-X25519 is the X-Wing construction. `draft-connolly-cfrg-xwing-kem` expired in September 2026 and `draft-irtf-cfrg-concrete-hybrid-kems` carries the same construction, under the same label, with published vectors; that is the document the implementation follows.

A hybrid KEM refuses the auth and auth-psk modes with `hpke/auth-unsupported`, at the sender and the recipient, for the reason ML-KEM does: neither defines an AuthEncap. A wrong-length seed, a public key or encapsulated key of any other total length, a `pkm` that is not the derivation of the supplied seed, and on the two prime-curve suites a traditional half that is not a point on the curve, are each refused with `hpke/bad-key` before any decapsulation runs. MLKEM768-X25519 has no point check to make, RFC 7748 sec. 5 making every 32-byte string a valid X25519 public key, and refuses a half that drives the agreement to the all-zero output.

`pki.possession.verifyRequest` takes `opts.intermediates`, the rest of the signature certificate's certification path, for the ordinary case where an intermediate CA issued that certificate rather than a trust anchor directly. It is ordered as `pki.path.validate` takes a path, from the certificate nearest an anchor down to the issuer of the signature certificate. Without it only a signature certificate an anchor issued itself can satisfy the RFC 9883 sec. 4 path-validation MUST.
Fixed: `pki.possession.verifyRequest` and `pki.possession.statementOf` check that the certificate a statement carries is the one its `signer` names, whichever way the statement reaches them. A request parsed by `pki.schema.csr.parse` carries the statement already decoded, and that record was returned without the check, so a request whose statement named one certificate while carrying another was accepted with `valid: true` even though the `signer` it reported did not identify the key that signed the request. Both routes now refuse it with `possession/signer-mismatch`.

`pki.x509.sign` and `pki.crl.sign` hold an alternative signing key to the same two checks the native one has always had. It must be the private half of `issuer.altPublicKey`: two different keys of one algorithm resolve to the same signature algorithm, so signing succeeded and emitted an artifact whose alternative signature did not verify under the key the issuer named. And `issuer.altPublicKey` must be the alternative key `issuer.cert` publishes in its `subjectAltPublicKeyInfo`, since that is the key a relying party reads to check an alternative signature; an issuer certificate that publishes none cannot sign an alternative signature at all. A self-signed certificate is held to the alternative key it publishes itself. Each is `x509/bad-input` or `crl/bad-input`.

`pki.tuf.canonicalJson` refuses a string carrying an unpaired UTF-16 surrogate, in an object key as well as a value. Such a code unit has no UTF-8 encoding and the conversion to bytes substituted U+FFFD for it, so two documents differing only there had identical signing bytes and a signature over one verified over the other while the document read back was the other one. It is now `tuf/bad-input`. A well-formed surrogate pair is an ordinary code point and still encodes.

`pki.tuf.verifySignatures` checks that a key's material is of the algorithm the key declares before verifying anything under it. A key's identifier is the hash of the whole key object, so its `keytype` and `scheme` are as authenticated as the material, but the PEM was imported and handed to the verifier as it stood: a key filed under `keytype: "ecdsa"` whose PEM held an RSA public key verified an RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 signature and reported `verified: true`. The keytype and scheme must now be a pair the specification lists, an EC key must be on the curve its scheme names, and an RSA key must be at least 2048 bits; a key that is not is `tuf/bad-key`.

`pki.tuf.updateRoot` judges expiry on the root the chain finishes on rather than on the trusted root before the walk, which is where the specification puts the freeze-attack check. A client offline long enough for its pinned root to lapse could not adopt a correctly signed unexpired successor, so recovering meant replacing the trust anchor by some other means; the same check on every intermediate root stopped a client catching up across older rotations. A chain that ends on an expired root, and a lapsed root with no successor to move to, are still `tuf/expired`.

`pki.sigstore.verifyBundle` holds a Rekor entry's `keyDetails` to the whole algorithm it names, not just the key family. Every NIST curve shares the `ecPublicKey` object identifier and every RSA size shares `rsaEncryption`, so comparing identifiers alone left the curve and the modulus size unchecked and an entry could state `PKIX_ECDSA_P384_SHA_384` over a P-256 key that signed with SHA-256. The curve an ECDSA name states and the modulus size an RSA name states are now checked against the leaf key, and a mismatch is `sigstore/entry-mismatch`.

A `keyDetails` name states a signature scheme too, and `PKIX_ED25519_PH` and the three `PKIX_RSA_PSS_*` names are now refused with `sigstore/bad-tlog-entry` rather than checked under a scheme they do not name. Signatures are verified with RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 and ordinary Ed25519, so an entry declaring RSA-PSS had a PKCS#1 v1.5 signature accepted for it and one declaring Ed25519ph an ordinary Ed25519 signature. Each becomes available once its scheme is carried into verification: RSA-PSS needs the padding and salt length threaded to the verify call, and Ed25519ph a pre-hashed Ed25519 the runtime does not offer.

`pki.tlog.verifyCheckpoint` and `pki.tlog.verifyNote` read the caller's bytes once, before anything is decoded, and verify that copy. Both took a view of the caller's buffer and held it across the Ed25519 key import the verification awaits, and `verifyCheckpoint` read the input a second time to decode the checkpoint, so a caller that reused or overwrote the buffer in that window could be handed `verified: true` alongside a tree size and root hash the signature never covered.

`pki.ct.verifySct`, `pki.ct.getProofByHash` and `pki.ct.getSthConsistency` copy the trust inputs a caller supplies before anything is awaited. `verifySct` digested the log key to match `sct.logId` and then read that key again to import it, so a caller reusing the buffer could satisfy the log-identity check with one key and have the signature verified under another. The proof clients held the tree head's root hash and the leaf hash across the network fetch, so a buffer reused during the fetch decided what the proof was folded against: an empty proof folds a one-leaf tree to its own leaf hash, which is enough to make a root overwritten mid-fetch accept a proof nobody vouched for.

`pki.ct.getSth` and `pki.ct.addChain` copy the pinned log key, and `addChain` the entry it submits, before the request goes out. Both read them again afterwards: the key is what the tree head or the returned SCT is verified under, and the entry is the preimage that SCT covers. A caller reusing either buffer during the request therefore had its receipt checked against a log it never pinned, or issued for bytes it never submitted.

`pki.sigstore.verifyBundle` refuses a Rekor entry whose `keyDetails` is present but not one of the names this build reads, including a number or an object. Only a string entered the algorithm checks, so any other type was passed over as though the entry had declared nothing, which made it the way past every check that an unknown name is refused by. Protobuf JSON permits an enum as its numeric value, so a number is a shape a producer emits. An omitted `keyDetails` still states nothing to hold and still verifies.

`pki.tuf.updateRoot` judges expiry at the instant supplied when validation began. A `Date` is mutable and the caller keeps theirs, and the freeze-attack check runs after a signature has been verified for every root in the chain, so a root that had expired by the instant given passed if that `Date` was moved back while the chain was walked.

`pki.tlog.verifyNote` and `pki.tuf.verifySignatures` copy the KEY material a caller supplies, not just the document, and derive each key's identifier from that copy. A note or a document with several signatures awaits a verification for each one while the key list is held, so a caller replacing a later key's bytes in that window had its identifier checked against one key and its signature verified under another: in a note, a signature line could be attributed to a signer whose key never signed it, and in TUF metadata a role's threshold could be met by material nobody authorized. `pki.tuf.verifySignatures` also copies the role, whose threshold is compared against the count once every signature has been checked.

`pki.possession.verifyRequest` decides the RFC 9883 section 4 prohibition on obtaining a signature certificate from the subject key as well as from the key usages a request asks for. It read only the usages, so omitting the `keyUsage` extension reported the prohibition as not engaged while asking to certify a key that can only sign, and such a key needs this mechanism for nothing. Every signature-only family the toolkit reads now engages it: EdDSA, RSASSA-PSS, the stateful hash-based algorithms, and the ML-DSA, SLH-DSA and composite ML-DSA families. A bare `rsaEncryption` key can do key transport and an EC key can agree, so those two are still decided by the usages the request names.

`pki.relatedCert.verifyRequest` verifies a proof made with an RSASSA-PSS key whose SubjectPublicKeyInfo restricts its hash. Deciding whether naming a digest would change the signature algorithm was done by resolving the algorithm at two digests and comparing, and one of those probes asked for SHA-512, which such a key refuses: the probe failed before the digest the caller asked for was resolved, and a valid proof under the key's own hash was reported as an unsupported algorithm. A restricted key is asked what it pins instead of probed, `digestAlgorithm` naming that hash is accepted, and naming a different one says which hash the key is restricted to.

`pki.ct.sthSignedData` accepts the tree-head record `pki.ct.getSth` returns. The record carries the log's own JSON document beside the decoded fields, and that field was refused as unknown, so asking for the bytes the log signed over a tree head just fetched threw instead of producing them.

`pki.ct.addChain` and `pki.ct.addPreChain` return the SCT in the shape the rest of the module reads, the one `pki.ct.parseSctList` produces: the algorithm bytes decoded, and `signature` the raw signature rather than the TLS digitally-signed structure it arrived in. A receipt is useful only if it can be embedded and re-verified, and it was in neither shape, so `pki.ct.encodeSctList` and `pki.ct.verifySct` both refused a receipt the log had just issued.

`pki.possession.verifyRequest` refuses a request that asks for a `subjectAltName` or `keyUsage` extension whose value does not decode, with `possession/bad-request`. An unreadable extension read as an absent one, so the two RFC 9883 section 4 name comparisons had nothing to compare and reported that the policy did not apply, while the request itself came back `valid: true`. A certification request's parser holds an extension's wrapper to its shape and not its decoded value, so nothing upstream refused it either.

`pki.tlog.parseVkey` accepts a verifier key whose base64 material contains `+`. Only the first two plus characters are separators, the name and key ID coming before them, and the rest of the line is base64 whose alphabet includes `+`; rejecting a third one refused most real Ed25519 verifier keys, a 44-character field carrying a plus more often than not. A key name containing a plus is still refused, since the field between the separators must be eight hex digits.

`pki.transport.peerChain` bounds a TLS handshake with an absolute deadline, the timer the request path already used, rather than with the socket's inactivity timeout. The two differ for a peer that keeps a connection busy without completing the handshake, and `timeout` is stated as a budget for the operation.

`pki.tlog.parseTilePath` bounds a tile index to the same uint64 range `pki.tlog.tilePath` emits. It accepted any number of index segments and multiplied a growing integer once per segment, so it read indices no writer can produce and a long path from an untrusted server cost work in proportion to its length. A path with more index segments than a uint64 index occupies, or naming a value above that range, is `tlog/bad-tile`, and the segment count is checked before any of them is read.
